sections.title: Plan shared responsibility without shared confusion
sections.text: Choose the monitored business email and identify who handles incoming notices. The county specifically recommends a generic address accessible to multiple individuals. Document administration and backup duties while following the portal’s security features. sections.title: Review business classifications thoughtfully
sections.text: The county asks registrants to select relevant NAICS codes so opportunities can be matched to their business. Describe the company’s actual products and services, then use the current portal and appropriate official classification references. Do not add unrelated categories simply to appear broader. Revisit selections if the business’s offerings change or alerts consistently miss the work you intend to pursue.

sections.title: Separate account setup from bid readiness
sections.text: A completed registration may allow the business to receive notices and respond electronically, but each solicitation can request different qualifications and documents. Assign a person to review the actual opportunity before a pricing commitment. Keep required items, unanswered questions and responsible contributors visible. Do not label the business approved for county work merely because the account is active.

sections.title: Use the right support channel
sections.text: The current Supplier’s Guide distinguishes registration support from assistance for existing vendors. Follow the contact information it publishes for the issue at hand. Keep a short description of the problem and any non-sensitive error details. Avoid emailing confidential identifiers or credentials when a support request can be explained without them; use the channel the authorized support team directs.

sections.title: Maintain the record after staff changes
sections.text: Imagine the employee who first registered the company leaves. The team should still know which email receives notices, who owns the account and where submission confirmations are stored. Review contact details during that transition. Preserve the current solicitation files and their status so an active opportunity is not lost merely because one person’s role changed.

sections.text: Maintain separate statuses for procurement portal registration, any certification application and a specific contract opportunity. One may be complete while another remains unresolved. sections.text: Ask for the current requirements before assembling or sending sensitive ownership and financial information. sections.text: Record any resource referral, event or technical-assistance step the division suggests. Name the person who will follow up and explain the question to resolve. sections.title: Bring a concise working document
sections.text: Prepare a short business summary, the decision being considered and the evidence gathered so far. For a marketing question, explain the offer, intended customer and what current inquiries show. For an operating question, describe the steps and where difficulties arise. Leave uncertain figures labeled as estimates rather than polishing them into misleading precision.

sections.title: Clarify the type of assistance
sections.text: The center describes general counseling and technical assistance across several business topics. Ask which format fits your request and what preparation is useful. sections.title: Respect appointment capacity

If several people from the business attend, decide who presents the question and who records actions so the session does not become a conflicting account of the same problem.

sections.title: Apply the advice to a small test
sections.text: Imagine an owner is uncertain which of two customer groups to pursue. The follow-up might be a defined set of interviews and a comparison of the findings, rather than an immediate branding overhaul. Keep the test, evidence and next decision together. sections.text: After a session, choose a practical exercise or research task. For a customer-discovery topic, that might mean drafting questions and reviewing them before conducting interviews. sections.text: The Swartz Center offers several programs with their own participation criteria. sections.title: Use a learning log for the team
sections.text: Suppose two colleagues attend a session on business models. Each can record one idea, one unresolved question and one experiment the business might try. title: Pitt Business Research Clinic: Prepare a Market Question

sections.text: Instead of asking whether your business will work, identify the information missing from the decision. sections.title: Define the market carefully
sections.text: Write down the proposed product or service, customer type and geographic area. Distinguish the people who use the offering from those who purchase it. The definition can change during research, but an explicit starting point makes the search reproducible.

sections.title: Use the official appointment route
sections.text: The library’s commercialization page links the research consultation scheduler. Follow that current route and check the available appointment details. Explain what information you already have and what you hope to learn. sections.title: Bring previous findings with provenance
sections.text: Save the source, date and definition behind any figures you already use. A market-size number is difficult to evaluate if its geography, industry boundary or year is missing. Share the question and the source rather than just a chart copied into a pitch deck. The research conversation can then address whether the evidence matches the decision.

sections.title: Record limits alongside findings
sections.text: A directory may help identify potential competitors but may omit recent changes. A demographic dataset may describe a population without measuring purchase intent. Do not convert the clinic’s assistance into a statement that the university endorses the business or its forecast.

sections.title: Use an example to organize follow-up
sections.text: Suppose a founder wants to offer a service to independent retailers. The clinic conversation could help define the retailer category and locate relevant sources. Keep the source-based findings separate from interview results and projections so later decisions show which kind of evidence supports each conclusion.

sections.text: Identify a decision-maker who can answer questions, explain the business context and review interim work. title: Carnegie Library Business Research: Turn a Market Question into a Search Plan
description: Prepare a focused research request using Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh business resources, with geography, dates and assumptions clearly defined.
intro: Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh’s business-resource guide points readers toward industry and market research, business planning, and help locating business information. For a Pittsburgh owner, the useful starting point is a precise research question. A database result can support a decision, but it does not establish customer demand for a particular shop, service or price. Use the library’s current resource and contact pages to confirm access and assistance.

sections.title: Write a decision before collecting statistics
sections.text: Describe what the business needs to decide and when. A proposed service territory, a new customer segment and a possible storefront require different evidence. sections.title: Define the place and population

If the resource cannot support the desired small-area detail, preserve that limitation rather than dividing a regional number into an invented neighborhood estimate. Ask which geographic definitions the source actually uses.

sections.title: Keep a source-and-date ledger
sections.text: For each useful result, save the source name, measurement period, retrieval date, definition and any access limitations. Separate a forecast from an observed count. A recent download can contain older underlying data, so the download date alone does not describe freshness. Keep enough citation detail to reproduce the search. Follow the resource’s permitted-use rules before redistributing extracts or placing licensed data in a public business plan.

sections.title: Compare like measures before making a chart
sections.text: Check whether two figures use the same time period, categories and units. If one source counts employers and another counts locations, explain the difference. Do not describe a mismatch as market growth without evidence. A small comparison table with definitions often reveals more than a polished chart. The owner can then identify which apparent opportunity rests on comparable information and which still needs a customer interview or another source.

sections.title: Separate desk research from customer evidence
sections.text: Library research can help frame a market, but it does not replace testing the actual offer. For the delivery example, broad population data would not establish willingness to order, acceptable prices or delivery economics. Record those as separate questions for appropriate research. Keep interview observations and transaction evidence labeled with their own limitations. Avoid turning a handful of enthusiastic comments into a statistical estimate of the whole neighborhood.

sections.title: Bring back a concise unresolved question
sections.text: After reviewing the initial material, return with the specific gap rather than asking for every available business statistic. Identify what was searched, which definition caused difficulty and what decision remains open. Keep the research file with the planning version it informed. The result should be a transparent evidence trail that another person can inspect, not a claim that the library endorses the business or guarantees a successful launch.

Keep each specialist question assigned to a suitable source of advice.

sections.title: Prepare a separate shipment brief
sections.text: For a forwarder discussion, organize origin, destination, goods description, dimensions, weight, dates and the services requested. Mark uncertain information clearly. Ask what the proposal includes, who handles each document and which charges remain outside the quote. Trade.gov lists multiple possible forwarding services; do not assume every provider includes all of them or uses the same commercial terms.

sections.title: Make the responsibility map visible
sections.text: Record the seller, buyer, forwarder and other relevant parties beside their agreed responsibilities. Ask qualified advisers about obligations that the team does not understand. Hiring an intermediary should not be treated as an automatic transfer of every exporter obligation. This guide organizes questions and records; it does not classify goods, determine license requirements or decide whether a transaction may proceed.

sections.title: Reconcile the plan before dispatch
sections.text: Compare the commercial assumptions with the shipment proposal and resolve inconsistencies through the appropriate parties. Save the agreed version and contact details for exceptions. title: Pittsburgh Nonprofit Coaching vs a Project Consultant

A nonprofit considering help should identify the decision it owns, the output it needs and the work its staff can perform before comparing the two approaches.

sections.title: State the leadership question separately
sections.text: A leader may need a confidential sounding board to examine priorities, board relationships or organizational choices. Write a short question that can be discussed without assuming an external adviser will make the decision. Confirm program fit and the arrangements for sharing sensitive information directly. Coaching should not be described to the board as an outsourced management function unless an actual agreement establishes that role.

sections.title: Name the project deliverable
sections.text: If the need is a completed analysis, facilitated process or implemented system, specify the output, audience and acceptance criteria. Ask a prospective consultant what is included and what remains the organization’s responsibility. A broad subject such as strategy does not tell you whether the assignment ends with discussion, a written plan or implementation support. Request examples of the form of deliverable without asking for another client’s confidential work.

sections.title: Compare the demand on staff time
sections.text: Coaching often depends on leaders bringing questions and acting on what they learn. A project also requires staff input, access and review even when a consultant produces the deliverable. Assign an internal owner and estimate the time available. If the organization has no capacity to implement recommendations, surface that constraint before investing effort in either route.

sections.title: Clarify authority and reporting
sections.text: Identify who approves the engagement, receives updates and accepts completion. Keep board decisions, management decisions and adviser suggestions distinguishable in the record. For a consultant, ask about scope changes, fees, confidentiality and ownership of work. For a coaching program, ask about participation and the limits of the support. Do not infer those terms from a program name or an introduction.

sections.title: Choose the sequence that resolves the need
sections.text: A leadership conversation can help define a later project, while a completed project may reveal a question worth discussing with a coach. Neither sequence guarantees funding or improved organizational results. Review what changed in the decision, what output was received and what actions remain. The useful comparison is whether the organization now has the support and capacity needed for its next specific step.

A listing, meeting or promotional mention should never be treated as evidence that a particular number of sales will follow.

sections.title: Read the phase before planning around it
sections.text: Checked November 21, 2026, the PDP page describes phase-one outreach and promotion, with later marketing-agency support planned for a second phase. Ask what is active, how participation works and which materials are useful before placing an outside agency assignment on hold.

sections.text: Write a question your operation can actually answer: are nearby office workers aware of the weekday pickup window, or are weekend visitors finding the entrance? sections.title: Prepare an accurate promotion packet

sections.title: Worked example: a weekday pickup test
sections.text: Imagine a fictional lunch shop with a staffed pickup window from noon until two. Its brief asks whether the PDP has a relevant channel for a two-week awareness test. The shop supplies an approved menu link, the exact dates and a named responder. It records pickup enquiries separately from completed orders. A busier week could reflect weather or another event; the owner therefore treats the result as a lead for further testing, not a calculated return attributable to PDP.

sections.title: Close the loop without assuming placement
sections.text: After an introductory conversation, record what was requested, who owns the next step and when information expires. If the answer is newsletter-only participation today, maintain the packet for that channel. If someone requests revisions, retain the approved version and send corrections promptly when hours change. Before commissioning paid creative work, clarify whether it is needed for the available opportunity and who owns the resulting files.

checklist: A single customer question and the observation behind it.
Approved public details, working mobile link and image-use permission.
Questions about the currently active phase and participation process.
One owner for approvals, corrections and a dated follow-up.

sections.title: Check the current opportunity first

sections.text: Explain what a visitor would do in the shop, what would be sold or demonstrated and what needs to happen behind the counter. Include an approximate footprint, storage needs and the number of people who would staff an ordinary day. This gives a reviewer useful constraints without asserting that a proposed use is already approved.

sections.title: Build a reversible setup plan
sections.text: Divide the proposed setup into portable equipment, removable displays and anything requiring building work. Identify power, internet, delivery and waste arrangements that need confirmation. Record who would maintain fixtures, replace damaged equipment and restore the premises. A low purchase price is not the whole setup cost: transport, assembly and removal can be substantial. Ask the property contact and appropriate reviewers which alterations require consent before committing to them.

sections.title: Worked example: an eight-week design shop
sections.text: A fictional maker wants to test a small collection through staffed demonstrations. Its first budget assumes eight weeks only for internal planning, not as an advertised program term. It lists portable shelving, inventory delivery, demonstration materials, staffing and removal. It also keeps an alternative plan with fewer events if the eventual space cannot support them. The maker asks whether the actual opportunity fits before turning that plan into a public launch schedule.

sections.title: Plan the ending as carefully as the opening
sections.text: Prepare a closeout checklist covering unsold goods, customer orders, keys, condition records and removal appointments. State what happens if the opportunity is shorter than expected or does not proceed. Any continued occupancy would need separate confirmation; success in a temporary test is not permission to remain. Keep a written list of questions about insurance, utilities, deposits, incentives and other obligations for the actual agreement.

checklist: A one-page concept with visitor activity, staffing and space needs.
Current-space and current-application questions for PDP.
Budget that does not assume an unawarded subsidy.

title: Paris to Pittsburgh: Prepare a Design-Funding Enquiry

Paris to Pittsburgh belongs in the funding conversation. A program enquiry does not replace a permit review, property-owner consent or a contractor’s scope. Keep these tracks separate so an encouraging conversation is not mistaken for authorization to start work.

sections.title: Use the current cycle, not an old deadline
sections.text: The PDP page checked November 21, 2026 says guidelines and funding limits changed on August 25, 2026. Its displayed schedule ends with a November 18 review and says there is no December meeting. Those dates do not establish a future submission window. Ask PDP for the next confirmed cycle and current instructions before preparing a dated application. Do not describe applications as open merely because an application PDF remains linked.

sections.title: Explain which exterior outcome you want
sections.text: The page distinguishes sidewalk-activation and façade improvements and describes a matching-grant structure. Identify whether a café element is part of the proposal or whether the work concerns the building frontage alone. Ask the program which current category and design materials fit your concept.

sections.title: Create a matching-fund question sheet
sections.text: List estimated design, supply, installation and other costs separately, with each estimate’s date and status. Identify which money is already available and which depends on someone else’s approval. Ask what costs, timing and evidence the current program accepts; do not silently treat every line of a contractor quote as eligible. Also ask about the sequence of review, agreement, work and payment. Keep the project viable on its own assumptions until an actual award and its conditions are documented.

sections.title: Worked example: a shopfront lighting proposal
sections.text: A fictional shop tenant wants new exterior lighting and a repaired entrance finish. Its file includes a landlord contact, condition photos, an initial designer sketch and two cost ranges. The tenant marks the sidewalk-café category as unresolved rather than choosing it to fit a headline benefit. It asks PDP about category fit and a future review date, while separately asking the relevant property and city contacts what approvals apply. No materials are ordered on the expectation of an award.

sections.title: Keep a decision record through revisions
sections.text: After the enquiry, save the current program documents and a short record of unanswered questions. Track changes to the design and budget together: a revised fixture choice may change both. Give each reviewer the same revision date, and identify who can approve spending. If the next cycle is not confirmed, maintain a ready file and a check-in date instead of inventing a deadline. This protects the project from old schedules circulating in forwarded emails.

Separate design, cost and permit-review tracks.
Written confirmation of the next available cycle before submitting.

title: Uptown Partners: Prepare a Business Directory Update

sections.title: Find the official submission route
sections.text: The Uptown Partners business page checked November 21, 2026 links a form for adding or updating a directory entry. It also offers a business-support contact route. Use the form linked from that page rather than a copied, unverified form address. Confirm whether your location and business type fit the directory’s current scope. sections.title: Resolve basic identity differences first
sections.text: Write the public trading name exactly as customers see it and keep any legal-entity explanation separate. Check the street number, suite and preferred arrival instructions against your own records. If the business operates by appointment or lacks a public walk-in location, say that plainly instead of supplying a convenient but misleading storefront address. Choose a public telephone and website that will remain available when a particular employee is away.

sections.title: Make hours and categories useful
sections.text: State ordinary hours separately from holiday changes, delivery hours and appointment windows. A general category should describe what a customer can obtain from the business, not every service you might offer someday. A concise description can explain a distinctive activity without unsupported superlatives. Avoid publishing credentials, accessibility features or service areas unless someone responsible has checked the exact statement. Keep temporary offers out of the evergreen description.

sections.title: Worked example: an appointment-only studio
sections.text: A fictional Uptown studio changes from walk-in retail to scheduled fittings. The update packet replaces the former open-door hours with an appointment statement, checks that the booking link works on a phone and identifies a public enquiry number. The owner includes a short change summary so a directory editor can see what needs replacing. After publication, the owner checks both the listing and the booking destination rather than assuming the submitted text was reproduced unchanged.

sections.title: Assign ongoing correction responsibility
sections.text: Save the submitted version, date and any acknowledgement in a shared business folder. Name someone to review the live entry after changes to hours, location or ownership. When correcting a record, identify the listing and the exact old and new text. Keep a change log so a second employee does not send a conflicting update. If a directory response is delayed, continue correcting your own website and customer messages through the channels you control.

checklist: Public trading name and verified customer-facing contact details.
Clear distinction between appointments, ordinary hours and exceptions.
One accurate category and a short factual description.
Submission copy, date and requested changes.
Named owner for live review and future corrections.

An enquiry is not a booked placement, paid campaign or promise of attendance.

sections.text: On the official organization page checked November 21, 2026, SDN invites submissions to marketing@sdnpgh.org for possible newsletter and social-media promotion. sections.text: Provide the business name, exact location, public destination link, concise event or product description and a contact for verification. Put the date, start and end time, price if any and booking conditions in distinct fields. Mark anything still provisional. If the request concerns a recurring event, identify the specific occurrence you want promoted. Check that the linked page carries the same facts so someone arriving from a shared post does not face contradictory instructions.

sections.title: Supply assets with permission and context
sections.text: Choose a clean image that remains legible on a small screen. State who owns it and whether the organization may crop or reproduce it for the proposed use. Include suggested descriptive text for a reader who cannot see the image. Avoid placing essential booking instructions only inside artwork. sections.title: Worked example: a repair workshop
sections.text: A fictional Strip District shop proposes a Saturday repair demonstration with twelve bookable places. The shop asks about editorial timing before assuming a newsletter appearance. sections.title: Measure the response you can observe
sections.text: Record the submission date, approved wording and any publication you actually see. If a tagged link is used, agree on it and check it before distribution. Count enquiries and bookings using your own records, while recognizing that other promotions can influence them. Thank the editor and send corrections promptly. title: State of the Strip: Build a Market-Evidence Reading File
description: Read the 2026 State of the Strip resource with explicit dates, geography and definitions before applying it to a business decision.
intro: A district report can help an owner form a better question about a location. It cannot establish the sales of a particular storefront. The State of the Strip resource is useful when each statistic remains attached to its actual geography, measurement period and definition. Build a reading file before copying numbers into a lease memo or business plan. A neatly formatted chart is still only as relevant as the population it measures.

sections.title: Separate the report year from the data year
sections.text: The official SDN resource page checked November 21, 2026 presents the 2026 report alongside earlier editions. Some observations describe an earlier calendar year or a period crossing two years. Record both publication edition and observation period for each figure you intend to use. Do not label every value as current simply because the report heading says 2026. Save a link and the relevant definition so another reader can trace the statement.

sections.title: Check geography before comparing properties
sections.text: The office section identifies a Pittsburgh Fringe submarket that includes several neighborhoods, not only the Strip District. That means a summarized office asking figure is not a quote for a particular Strip building. Record the geographic unit beside the number and compare it with the location of the business decision. If two sources use different boundaries, present them separately until you can establish a meaningful common basis.

sections.title: Read activity counts with their definitions
sections.text: The visitor discussion includes a methodological note about some in-person employees being counted as visitors. That category is therefore not interchangeable with unique shoppers, purchases or people who passed one entrance. Likewise, properties in a development pipeline are different from completed, occupied buildings. Treat these as separate observations. Avoid adding categories together when they might overlap, and do not turn planned inventory into confirmed future demand for your business.

sections.title: Worked example: selecting shop observation periods
sections.text: A fictional retailer uses the report to ask whether weekday and weekend conditions deserve separate on-site observations. It creates three columns: report observation, remaining question and evidence to collect. A broad visitor count leads to a question about activity outside its proposed entrance; a pipeline reference leads to a question about project status. The owner then schedules its own observations and asks for current property-specific information. It does not multiply the district count by an assumed conversion rate to claim store revenue.

sections.title: Turn uncertainties into a review agenda
sections.text: Mark each planned use of evidence as supported, uncertain or irrelevant to this decision. For an apparent anomaly, seek the underlying report or ask the publisher before repeating it. Preserve the original wording rather than silently fixing a surprising value. Use the file in discussions with advisers and property representatives, with clear questions about gaps. A defensible decision memo explains what the report informed and what still required separate verification.

checklist: Edition, observation period and source link for every selected figure.
Geographic boundary and unit beside each value.
Visitor, employee, completed and pipeline definitions kept separate.
Questions for a property-specific enquiry or on-site observation.
No unsupported conversion from district activity to store sales.

sections.text: The membership page checked November 21, 2026 groups business dues by employee count and lists separate resident, nonprofit and landlord categories. Verify the current amount and which classification applies directly through the official membership route. Ask how employees are counted if your staffing pattern makes the category unclear, and confirm the covered period and renewal process. sections.text: A fictional four-person studio wants stronger neighborhood connections and accurate discovery information. Decide whether to renew using the confirmed service and your experience rather than a general expectation of guaranteed exposure.

Published benefits separated from common district work.
Staff owner and realistic participation time.
Any separate submission or event requirements.
A review record that distinguishes observed introductions from assumed referrals.

title: Lawrenceville Together: Route a Business-Support Question

sections.text: The organization page checked November 21, 2026 says Lawrenceville Corporation and Lawrenceville United merged in January 2026 under Lawrenceville Together. sections.text: Decide whether you need neighborhood information, help locating a resource, a connection about a shared concern or a defined professional service. sections.title: Worked example: a retailer with a delivery concern
sections.text: A fictional Lawrenceville retailer has recurring confusion about delivery arrivals. Its initial note gives the location, ordinary delivery window and a factual description of the issue without identifying customers. It asks which current neighborhood or city contact should receive the operational question. If referred onward, the retailer records the handoff and sends a focused follow-up. One decision and the specific help requested.
Brief business context and a factual time constraint.
Referral owner, next step and current-source verification.
